desc:
Split the elements of nums into groups. A group may contain any elements (they do not have to be next to each other in the array, and the order inside a group is irrelevant), but the largest minus the smallest value in a group must be at most k. Every element belongs to exactly one group.

Return the minimum number of groups needed. For an empty array the answer is 0.

nums = [3, 6, 1, 2, 5], k = 2 -> 2   ({1,2,3} and {5,6})
nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 1       -> 2   ({1,2} and {3})
nums = [4, 4, 4], k = 0       -> 1
hints: The positions in the array do not matter, so you are free to reorder the values.
After sorting, a group that is as good as any other can always be a contiguous block of the sorted order.
Start a group at the smallest unassigned value v and absorb every value up to v + k. The first value beyond v + k starts the next group.
editorial: Because only values matter, sort the array. Take the smallest unassigned value v. It must belong to some group, and that group can only contain values in [v, v + k]; making the group take all remaining values in that interval is never worse, since those values would otherwise have to be placed in other groups that could also be merged into this one (the spread of the merged group is still at most k).

So scan the sorted array, remember the start of the current group, and open a new group whenever a value exceeds start + k. The number of groups opened is the answer. Sorting gives O(n log n); the scan is linear.
